introduction_markdown: Answer BOTH sections in the SAME answer booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Begin with SECTION A. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. In the Directed Writing question avoid indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer because this will earn you no marks. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Time allowed: two hours.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A - DIRECTED WRITING (30 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content (14 marks); Expression and Accuracy (12 marks); Slanting (04 marks).

You are the workers' Representative of Cameroon Iron and Steel Industry, Tiko, which is plagued by gossip, a situation that affects productivity negatively. You intend to give a talk to your co-workers on what they should do to put an end to gossip as they celebrate the upcoming Labour Day.

Selecting relevant information from the points below, write in ONE paragraph of not more than **150 words**, in a convincing manner, paying attention to grammar, spelling, punctuation and handwriting.

- Gossip is the exchange of personal information about an absent third party that is conveyed in an evaluative manner.
- Do not participate; walk away from the gossip.
- Give visual clues that you are interested in listening to a gossip.
- Sometimes people use the gossip to bring someone down; usually someone who has something others want; e.g power, reputation or money.
- Change the topic when a friend wants to have a gossip session or tactfully talk about something else.
- Man is a social being and gossip is a social activity. Everyone then has the propensity to gossip.
- Be busy. If you are preoccupied with your work you cannot be available for the latest story.
- When someone confides in you about someone else, question it.
- Gossip can have many diverse effects on an organisation and most of all on individual reputation.
- Do not believe something unless you have clear proof.
- Through gossip people seem particularly pleased to discover and discuss the faults and weaknesses of others.
- Share information with people sparingly until you are sure that you have built a level of trust with them.
- Choose your friends at work wisely.
- Gossip results in the boss of an organisation spending an enormous amount of time trying to figure out who said what and to whom.
- Do not trust personal information with co-workers because if they gossip about others, they may gossip about you.
- Confidently tell a gossip that such behaviour is making things uncomfortable for you and other co-workers.
- There are people who are just plain vicious and would start a gossip without any particular reason.
- We need to be able to trust our friends and gossiping can break this trust.
- Befriend the gossip monger. If you notice someone who consistently gossips go close to him/her.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model answer (one paragraph, 148 words)**

Dear colleagues, as we celebrate Labour Day, let us resolve to put an end to the gossip that is hurting productivity in our industry. Gossip is the exchange of personal information about an absent person, and it can damage individual reputation and force our boss to waste an enormous amount of time finding out who said what. First, do not participate: walk away, and never give visual clues that you are interested. When a friend wants a gossip session, tactfully change the topic. Stay busy, because a worker who is preoccupied with his task has no time for the latest story. Do not believe anything without clear proof, and question whoever confides in you about someone else. Share personal information sparingly, choose your friends at work wisely, and confidently tell the gossip that such behaviour makes us uncomfortable. Together we can build a workplace of trust. Thank you.

**Why this works (selection and slanting).** The task is a talk on what workers should DO to end gossip, so the answer keeps the bullets that give advice (walk away, change the topic, stay busy, ask for proof, share information sparingly, choose friends wisely, speak up confidently) and adds only two background points (the definition and the damage to reputation and to the boss's time) to justify the appeal. It drops the bullets that point in the wrong direction or do not serve the purpose: "Give visual clues that you are interested in listening" and "Befriend the gossip monger" are the opposite of the advice needed, and "Man is a social being...", "people use gossip to bring someone down", "pleased to discover the faults of others", "plain vicious" and "trust our friends" are explanations of why gossip exists, not actions. The tone is direct and convincing (greeting, Labour Day, call to action, thanks), the sentences are rephrased in the candidate's own words, and everything is in a single paragraph under 150 words.

**Marking guide**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content | 14 | Relevant points chosen from the list (about 7 to 9 well-chosen points), in the right register for a talk to co-workers; no irrelevant or contradictory points |
| Expression and Accuracy | 12 | Own words (no lifting of whole bullets), varied linking, correct grammar, spelling and punctuation, ONE paragraph, 150 words at most |
| Slanting | 4 | Every point is turned into advice on how to END gossip and the speaker addresses colleagues convincingly (Labour Day, workers' representative) |

**Common mistakes**

1. Copying the bullets word for word: the instructions say indiscriminate copying earns no marks.
2. Including bullets that encourage gossip ("give visual clues that you are interested", "befriend the gossip monger") or that only explain why people gossip, so the talk is not slanted to its purpose.
3. Writing several paragraphs, a letter or a speech with headings, or going over 150 words.
